title: Find the slow part of a request

steps.caption: A request begins. Its response time includes each sequential stage.
Application work adds 70 ms before the database call.
Sequential total: 30 + 70 + 100 = 200 ms. This is one request latency.
A suitable index reduces only the query stage: 100 ms becomes 25 ms.
New total: 125 ms. More completed requests per second is a separate measure.

title: DNS: a name becomes an address

steps.caption: The browser needs the address for shop.example.
On a miss, the resolver follows DNS delegation to the responsible server.
The resolver returns the address and caches it for its TTL.
The browser can now connect to the web server. DNS did not carry the page.
A later lookup may use the cached answer until its TTL expires.

title: Lost data: transport choices

steps.caption: TCP presents an ordered byte stream; a lost segment can delay delivery.
TCP detects loss and retransmits; later bytes wait for the missing data.
UDP sends datagrams without a built-in delivery or ordering guarantee.
Datagram C can arrive without transport waiting for B.
The UDP application chooses whether to recover, ignore, or reorder data.

title: Scale a service without losing sessions

steps.caption: The client sends a request to the service entry point.
The load balancer routes the first request to App A.
App A keeps session state outside its own process.
A later request can be routed to App B.
App B retrieves the session instead of relying on App A memory.
More app instances do not remove shared-store bottlenecks or failures.

title: Cache-aside: hit, miss, and update

steps.caption: The application checks the cache for product 42.
On a miss, the application reads the authoritative database.
The application fills the cache for later reads.
A write changes the database to 550; the cached copy is now old.
Invalidate the old entry, then reload on a later miss. Races still need a policy.

title: Replication is copying, not partitioning

steps.caption: Both copies initially show address V1.
A write commits V2 on the primary.
Before replication applies, a replica read can still return V1.
The replication stream applies the update on the replica.
Both now show V2. Deletions can replicate too; replication is not a backup.

title: Two buyers, one remaining ticket

steps.caption: There is one unit of product 42. Both buyers want it.
A performs an atomic update WHERE product_id = 42 AND quantity > 0.
B executes the same conditional update after A.
Only A may confirm a reservation from these results.
Related changes need a suitable transaction; external payment is another boundary.

title: An address update and duplicated data

steps.caption: A normalized current view refers to the customer rather than copying every field.
An order can also retain the delivery address used at purchase time.
The customer changes their current address to B.
A live join sees B; the past delivery snapshot should still show A.
Choose duplication by meaning and access pattern, not a universal rule.

title: Sharding divides ownership of data

steps.caption: Choose a shard from the customer identifier.
Customer 42 is routed to A.
Customer 1500 is routed to B, not to a duplicate of A.
A replica of A copies A data, not B data.
A query across both customer ranges needs deliberate coordination.

title: Consistent hashing: a node joins

steps.caption: Keys go clockwise to the next node. Key K at 170 maps to C at 260.
K is owned by C before the new node joins.
D joins at 200 degrees, between B and C.
K at 170 now meets D first. Move the affected range from C to D.
A key at 80 still maps to B. Not every key needs to move.

title: Bloom filter: no, or maybe

steps.caption: Insert A with illustrative hash positions 1, 4, and 8.
A query needing bit 2 finds zero: definitely absent from the represented set.
A different key X can map to bits 1, 4, and 8 too.
Verify a positive result in real storage; a collision can mean X is absent.
The filter saves absent-key reads, but is not the final membership authority.

title: CAP: a choice during a partition

steps.caption: Both replicas initially know that a ticket is available.
A records sold, then communication to B is unavailable.
A request reaches non-failing B, which cannot confirm the current state at A.
Choice 1: answer without the latest write; consistency may be sacrificed.
Choice 2: refuse or wait; CAP availability is sacrificed for this request.

title: PACELC: normal operation also matters

steps.caption: Normal operation: waiting for distant coordination can cost latency.
Coordinated completion can provide the chosen stronger guarantee.
An asynchronous path can respond sooner while the remote copy lags.
During a partition, availability versus consistency becomes a separate choice.

title: A saga compensates a completed step

steps.caption: Record a pending order and a recoverable step identifier.
A local payment operation commits successfully.
Stock reservation fails. Earlier committed work did not vanish.
The saga issues a compensating refund with safe retry behavior.
Record completion after confirmation; compensation can take time or fail too.

title: LRU and FIFO make different choices

steps.caption: Insert A, B, and C into caches with room for three equal-size entries.
Read A. LRU updates recency; FIFO keeps insertion order.
Insert D. LRU evicts B, the least recently used entry.
FIFO evicts A, the earliest inserted entry.
Eviction frees memory. It does not establish that a cached price is current.

title: A lost response must not mean two charges

steps.caption: The client sends one payment attempt with idempotency key K.
Atomically associate K with one payment operation and its recoverable result.
The response is lost after the operation succeeds.
The client retries using K and the same request body.
Return or resume the recorded result, rather than create a second charge.

title: Token bucket: bursts have a limit

steps.caption: This illustrative bucket holds three tokens and refills at one token/second.
Request 1 consumes a token and is allowed.
Two more requests consume the remaining tokens.
A new immediate request is rejected or delayed by the chosen policy.
After one second, one token is available again, up to the bucket capacity.

title: Which way do live updates travel?

steps.caption: Long polling: browser sends a request; the server may hold its response.
A response arrives; the browser starts another request for later updates.
Separate SSE example: server events arrive over a streaming HTTP response.
Separate WebSocket example: after setup, the browser can send a message.
The server can send messages back on the same WebSocket connection.

title: A work queue can redeliver a job

steps.caption: One logical job enters a queue shared by competing workers.
Worker A receives J and writes the result.
A crashes before acknowledging. The queue may redeliver J.
Worker B receives J and checks the durable result or deduplication rule.
Safe repeated processing avoids a duplicate business effect.

title: Independent subscribers need their own copy

steps.caption: Publish OrderPlaced once to a topic.
The billing subscription receives its own logical delivery.
The shipping subscription receives its own logical delivery.
Workers within one subscription may compete; independent subscriptions do not.
Timing and delivery guarantees depend on the broker and configuration.

title: CDC: a committed change reaches a read view

steps.caption: A database transaction commits a product price change.
The connector reads the corresponding durable-log position.
A change record reaches the stream; downstream work can lag.
The consumer applies the change using an appropriate id/version rule.
Recovery may replay records. Consumers must handle duplicates safely.

title: Event sourcing: replay builds state

steps.caption: Append Deposited(100) to the durable event history.
Apply the event to the derived balance.
Append Withdrawn(30), then update the view.
The current balance is 70.
Replay rebuilds the view; avoid repeating external side effects such as email.

title: CQRS: a read view can lag behind a write

steps.caption: A command creates order 42 in the write model.
An update event waits for processing.
A list read can temporarily show the old view.
The projector applies the update to the read view.
CQRS separates read and write responsibilities; event sourcing is optional.

title: Circuit breaker: closed, open, half-open

steps.caption: Closed: calls reach the dependency and failures are measured.
The configured failure rule opens the circuit.
During the open interval, new calls use a safe fallback or fail explicitly.
After a delay, half-open allows limited probe calls.
Successful probes can close it; failing probes can open it again.

title: Discovery data can become stale

steps.caption: A and B register reachable endpoints; health information is refreshed.
The caller discovers candidate orders endpoints.
A fails after discovery; a previously returned endpoint can now be stale.
A health timeout marks A suspect; the registry can stop advertising it.
A retry to B must respect the operation retry/idempotency policy.

title: Recovery time and data-loss targets differ

steps.caption: A recoverable backup exists at 10:00.
The service fails at 10:20; newer data may need another recoverable log.
Without newer recoverable data, this scenario loses up to 20 minutes.
Restore and validation take until 11:00.
Observed recovery took 40 minutes. RPO/RTO are targets, not these observations.

title: OAuth / OIDC: code, tokens, and audiences

steps.caption: The browser signs in at the provider; the client does not receive that password.
An authorization-code flow returns a code to the client redirect.
The client exchanges the code with the required checks, such as PKCE.
With OIDC, the client can receive an ID token; an access token targets an API.
The API validates the access token and enforces authorization.

title: SSO does not mean one universal app session

steps.caption: The user authenticates at the identity provider.
Payroll establishes its own application session using the sign-in result.
Email can reuse the provider session for sign-in, then create its own session.
Logging out of payroll may end only the payroll session.
Global logout needs an explicit plan for provider and application sessions.

title: TLS identity is separate from authorization

steps.caption: During TLS setup, the client validates the server certificate and identity.
The protected connection carries application traffic.
With mTLS, the server also validates a client certificate.
An authenticated client still needs permission for the requested operation.
Valid identity does not grant unlimited access to every record.

title: Nearby search must cross cell boundaries

steps.caption: A rider is close to the edge of cell A.
The nearest driver is across the boundary in cell B.
Searching only A misses that driver.
Search intersecting neighbor cells, then filter by actual distance.
Grid prefixes and quadtrees are candidate indexes, not exact distance tests.

title: Raft: minority isolation stops safe progress

steps.caption: A is leader in this illustrative three-voter crash-fault group.
Raft replicates and commits entries using its log, term, and majority rules.
A becomes isolated. A alone cannot commit conflicting new decisions.
B and C can elect a leader when protocol and timing conditions permit.
Only the communicating majority can progress under the protocol rules.

title: Lease expiry does not stop the old worker

steps.caption: A receives ownership token 10, then pauses.
A lease expires; B acquires a newer token 11.
The store accepts B and records the newer fencing token.
A resumes and sends a stale write carrying token 10.
The store rejects 10 because it enforces fencing. Issuing tokens alone is not enough.

title: Gossip spreads knowledge gradually

steps.caption: A learns a new membership observation, version V2.
A exchanges information with B.
B later exchanges with C; D may still have old information.
A reachable peer exchange eventually reaches D under convergence assumptions.
Spreading observations is not consensus on one committed transaction history.

title: A replacement helps only if traffic reaches it

steps.caption: Two app instances can handle the same request contract.
The router initially selects A.
A stops responding. A second box alone does not redirect traffic.
A configured health and routing policy switches suitable traffic to B.
Test shared dependencies too. Both apps can fail if their common database fails.

title: An index narrows the records to examine

steps.caption: Find orders for customer 7 in a hypothetical table with one million rows.
Without a useful access path, the engine may inspect the full table.
A suitable index maps customer 7 to candidate records.
Read or validate the matching records as required by the execution plan.
The index costs storage and write maintenance; measure the actual query plan.

title: CDN: origin miss, then nearby reuse

steps.caption: A viewer requests a public video segment from the nearby edge.
On a miss, the edge obtains the allowed content from the origin.
The edge stores the response according to its caching policy.
A later viewer request can be served without another origin fetch.
Versions, expiry, and access rules still matter. Private files need protection.

title: Peers share verified pieces and may leave

steps.caption: A trusted file description identifies the pieces and their expected digests.
C downloads a useful piece from A and verifies it.
C obtains another useful piece from B.
A leaves before sending piece 2. Discovery must locate another source.
Peers reduce origin traffic only when useful sources remain reachable.

title: Design example: create and resolve a short URL

steps.caption: Creation: validate the destination and allocate a short key with a collision policy.
Persist K -> destination under a uniqueness rule before confirming creation.
Resolution: a later request for K checks the fast lookup cache.
On a miss, retrieve the mapping and fill the cache using a freshness policy.
The service returns an HTTP redirect; the client requests the destination.
Later cache hits reduce mapping reads; expiry, deletion, and abuse still need policies.

title: Design example: accepted is not yet delivered

steps.caption: The sender submits one logical message using a stable message identifier.
Persist the message and recovery state before promising durable acceptance.
Acknowledge acceptance, which is different from recipient delivery.
Use a recoverable handoff for delivery work; do not lose work between stores.
An online recipient receives M42; offline clients need later retrieval.
A retry or reconnect can repeat M42. Deduplicate at the durable/client boundary.

title: Design example: fanout makes feeds fast, at a cost

steps.caption: Persist a new post with its author and stable identifier.
Schedule recoverable fanout work rather than blocking on every follower.
Fanout updates follower timelines, which can temporarily lag.
A reader asks the feed service for a bounded page.
Read prepared timeline references, then retrieve authorized post content.
Very large authors may need another fanout policy; a hybrid trades write work for read work.

title: Design example: prepare video, then serve nearby

steps.caption: An uploaded video is kept in durable object storage.
Encoding work creates suitable versions and segments; retries must be safe.
Prepared segments become available to the origin delivery path.
A viewer requests a segment from the CDN edge.
On a miss, the edge fetches allowed content from the origin.
Nearby reuse reduces origin delivery load; cold caches and access control still matter.

title: Design example: near a rider does not mean available

steps.caption: The rider requests a trip with a pickup location.
Search intersecting spatial cells and filter by actual distance and freshness.
Check current availability and conditionally claim the driver.
Notify the selected driver and track acceptance or timeout.
Another request must not also claim D. Stale location data is not an assignment guarantee.
Expired offers need an explicit release/retry policy before another assignment.

title: Interleaving is different from simultaneous execution

steps.caption: One execution unit starts A. Both tasks need two model time units of CPU work.
The same execution unit switches to B. Task lifetimes overlap, but work is interleaved.
It resumes A, which finishes after its second unit of work.
It resumes B. Both tasks finish after four model time units.
Separate alternative: two available execution units run A and B at the same time.
Both finish after two model units in this idealized CPU-only example.

title: Batch and streaming organize the same arrivals differently

steps.caption: Compare two alternatives for the same arriving records.
E1 waits for a batch boundary; a streaming path can begin E1 now.
E2 joins the buffer; the streaming path can handle it as it arrives.
At its boundary, the batch processor receives the accumulated group.
Batching amortizes overhead but adds waiting. Streaming still has processing delay.

title: Read-through and write-through can be combined

steps.caption: Read-through: the application asks the cache layer for a missing value.
The cache layer loads it from the backing database.
The layer caches V1 and returns it to the application.
Write-through: the application sends a new value through that layer.
The layer synchronously persists the write according to its write policy.
After the required writes succeed, acknowledge. Failure ordering still needs a policy.

title: Who initiates the update: sender or receiver?

steps.caption: Both alternatives begin with the receiver knowing version V1.
The provider records V2 and initiates a push notification.
The polling receiver can remain on V1 until its next check.
The polling receiver initiates a request asking for updates.
The pull response now supplies V2. Poll interval and retry behavior affect delay.

title: An order response can precede email completion

steps.caption: A client submits an order request.
Persist the order and recoverable email work record under the required atomic rule.
Asynchronous choice: acknowledge order creation, not email completion.
A recoverable handoff queues email work.
The worker can finish the email later and must tolerate retries.
Separate synchronous choice: the caller waits for required downstream work.
That response is delayed by the downstream result and its failure behavior.
